title: Place changes the route into public life more than the overall level of engagement
source_unit: Pew Research Center and Pew-Knight Initiative, How urban, suburban and rural Americans engage in society
geography: United States; urban, suburban, and rural adults

observations.period: September 8–14, 2025; publication September 28, 2026; engagement groups by community type

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Wave 179 of the American Trends Panel; group shares exclude adults not assigned to a group

urban_groups.unit: percent of urban adults assigned to each engagement group

suburban_groups.unit: percent of suburban adults assigned to each engagement group

rural_groups.unit: percent of rural adults assigned to each engagement group

place_route_mechanism.value: Urban, suburban, and rural settings show broadly similar overall engagement distributions but different mixes of civic, religious, news, and political practice

observations.method: Pew Wave 179 of the American Trends Panel, surveyed by web and phone September 8–14, 2025; engagement groups were assigned using a separate Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey cluster analysis based on 19 measures.
observations.uncertainty: The source is cross-sectional and group assignment is analytical rather than an enduring identity. Adults not assigned to a group are not shown in the displayed percentages; community type may proxy composition, access, age, income, or local institutions.
observations.subgroup: Urban, suburban, and rural U.S. adults classified as Mobilizers, Connectors, Spectators, or Outsiders.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small differences in group distributions should not be read as a meaningful urban-rural civic divide; the source explicitly notes that age, income, race, ethnicity, and party often predict behavior better than community type.

observations.period: September 8–14, 2025; publication September 28, 2026; social, religious, and group participation

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Wave 179 of the American Trends Panel

volunteered.unit: percent volunteering in the past year

group_membership.unit: percent part of a group or organization in the past year

monthly_religious_attendance.unit: percent attending religious services in person or online at least monthly

participation_route.value: Place-specific differences appear more clearly in social and religious participation than in the broad engagement-group distribution

observations.method: Pew Wave 179 self-reported activity measures; activities refer to the past 12 months.
observations.uncertainty: The reference period includes much of the 2024 presidential-election cycle; self-reports do not establish frequency, intensity, access conditions, or causal effects of place.
observations.subgroup: Urban, suburban, and rural adults; online religious attendance is included with in-person attendance in the published measure.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher rural religious attendance or suburban group membership may reflect population composition, institutional supply, or reporting differences rather than stronger generalized social connection.

observations.period: September 8–14, 2025; publication September 28, 2026; in-person versus online group interaction

denominator.unit: U.S. adults who belong to a group, organization, or association; subgroup base not stated on the article summary

group_mostly_in_person.unit: percent saying group members mostly interact in person

group_mixed_mode.unit: percent saying interaction is an equal mix of in-person and online

group_mostly_online.unit: percent saying group members mostly interact online

social_infrastructure_mechanism.value: Community type is associated with the medium through which organized social life is experienced, even where overall engagement levels are similar

observations.method: Pew Wave 179 question among group members about whether their group mostly interacts in person, online, or through an equal mix.
observations.uncertainty: The subgroup denominator is not headlined in the accessible summary; interaction mode is not the same as relationship quality, inclusion, accessibility, or durable belonging.
observations.subgroup: Adults belonging to a group, organization, or association, compared by urban, suburban, and rural residence.
observations.counterinterpretation: More in-person interaction may reflect fewer alternatives or local organizational norms rather than greater cohesion; online interaction can be meaningful and accessible for people otherwise excluded.

observations.period: September 8–14, 2025; publication September 28, 2026; place-specific political expression

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Wave 179 of the American Trends Panel

contacted_official.unit: percent contacting an elected official in the past year

displayed_sign_or_bumper.unit: percent displaying a sign/bumper sticker or wearing something for a candidate or cause

social_media_political_identity.unit: percent using a social-media bio or profile picture to support a candidate or cause

protest_participation.unit: percent participating in a protest, march, or demonstration

political_style_mechanism.value: Place is more visible in the form of political expression—signage, online identity, protest, or official contact—than in a single overall engagement score

observations.method: Pew Wave 179 reported political-activity measures for urban, suburban, and rural adults.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported activities over the prior year and do not establish political influence, issue content, persistence, or why different forms are chosen.
observations.subgroup: Urban, suburban, and rural adults; differences may reflect local political competition, organizational opportunity, social visibility, or demographic composition.
observations.counterinterpretation: Similar rates of contacting officials alongside different protest or signage rates show that visible political style is not equivalent to political efficacy or civic commitment.

related_sources.claim: Pew chart data provide the engagement-group percentages by community type.
Pew chart data provide the in-person, mixed, and online interaction comparison for group members.

boundary: This record adds a place-specific route into the existing public-life engagement typology. It does not establish an urban-rural civic divide, causality, durable belonging, institutional trust, political efficacy, or that in-person interaction is intrinsically better than online participation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official Pew Research Center article HTML reviewed for publication metadata, survey samples, engagement-group composition, activity comparisons, interaction medium, and stated place/composition limitations.
reproduction_audit.version_note: The article draws on Wave 179 and the Cross-Sectional Engagement Survey; those sources and chart CSVs should be used for exact subgroup reproduction.
